title: How to Keep Customer Feedback Trend Lines Comparable When the Survey, Taxonomy, or AI Model Changes
summary: Survey rewording, taxonomy edits and AI model swaps all break feedback trends. Five steps to keep them comparable, from one code frame to re-baselining history.
body_markdown:
The chart says billing complaints are up four points since Q1. Since Q1, someone also reworded the open-ended question. An analyst merged two themes. The vendor moved to a newer language model. Any one of those can move the number on its own, and nobody can tell the board which part of the four points is customers and which part is method.


You keep customer feedback trend lines comparable by holding the measurement constant and moving history with every definition change. That takes five habits. Run every question and wave on one code frame. Version the taxonomy and batch its changes. Re-baseline history instead of splicing old and new definitions. Build warehouse and BI tables that survive a theme change. Treat any AI model change as a change of method. Thematic handles the re-baseline inside the platform: when you merge, rename, or restructure themes, Thematic re-analyzes all existing feedback against the new structure, so old and new data carry the same themes.


Below is each step and the mistakes that most often break a tracker.


## The five-step process


1. **Use one code frame across every question and wave.** One theme set, applied to all open-ended questions and all periods.
2. **Version the taxonomy and batch the changes.** Edits go into a draft, get applied on a schedule, and get announced.
3. **Re-baseline history under the current frame.** Re-theme the back catalog so the whole series uses today's definitions.
4. **Make the warehouse and BI layer survive a theme change.** Replace history on re-theme instead of appending new labels beside old ones.
5. **Treat an AI model change as a methodology change.** Ask for notice, run old and new side by side, and restate if the gap is material.


## Step 1: Put every question and wave on one code frame


Survey researchers treat the first rule as settled.[Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/writing-survey-questions/) puts it plainly: "Because slight modifications in question wording can affect responses, identical question wording should be used when the intention is to compare results to those from earlier surveys."


Commercial trackers rarely keep wording frozen. That's survivable if the coding of the answers stays constant. It isn't when each question carries its own topic model.


Per-question topic models are common. Qualtrics Text iQ, for example, builds topics inside an individual question, with a documented limit of 350 parent topics and 350 topics per question. A tracker with ten open-ended questions ends up with ten topic sets that drift apart. Replace a question and its topic set starts from nothing. So does its trend line.


The fix is one code frame that sits above the questionnaire. In Thematic, a[Lens](https://getthematic.com/insights/lenses-context-layer-customer-intelligence) combines one or more datasets and analyzes them together with a single, unified set of themes. You can include several comment columns from the same survey. When you add a new data source to an existing Lens, it automatically picks up the Lens's themes. A reworded question becomes a new input to an existing frame, not a new frame.


Log each wording change as a dated note on the series.


## Step 2: Version the taxonomy and batch the changes


A code frame that never changes goes stale. Thematic's guide to[building a feedback taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) names the trade-off. Change the taxonomy constantly and you can't report trends over time. Freeze it and you miss emerging issues.


The answer is governance, not a freeze:


- **One owner.** A named person approves structural edits.
- **Drafts, not live edits.** Changes accumulate in a draft and apply as one release.
- **A schedule.** Batch structural changes monthly or quarterly, not ad hoc.
- **A change note.** Each release records what merged, split, or moved, and why.


Thematic's Themes Editor follows this pattern. Edits save to a draft and only reach the data when someone clicks Apply themes. Revert Draft rolls back to any of the last three applied versions and shows who applied each one and when. New themes found during maintenance wait for you to review and approve them, because a new theme changes every analysis already built on it. Thematic's help documentation suggests a simple message for stakeholders: "each quarter we run a discovery to improve the themes."


**Common mistake:** relying on the tool's revert history as your change log. Three versions cover a quarter of monthly releases at most. Keep your own dated log.


## Step 3: Re-baseline history instead of splicing it


The damaging move is to apply a new definition from today forward and leave history on the old one. The chart then joins two different measures, and any step at the change date is an artifact.


Official statisticians solve this by restating history. Eurostat's 2025[backcasting manual](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-manuals-and-guidelines/w/ks-01-25-030) is written for producers of official statistics "that need to produce consistent historical time series for an updated classification."


Feedback programs can do this more directly, because the raw comments are still there. Re-theme the entire back catalog under the current frame. Thematic does this automatically.[Merge, rename, or restructure a theme](https://getthematic.com/insights/customize-ai-themes-customer-feedback) and Thematic re-analyzes all existing feedback against the new structure. A comment tagged "Delivery problems" last month appears under "Shipping issues" once the two are merged. Thematic also[imports historical feedback](https://getthematic.com/insights/migrate-off-medallia-qualtrics) and analyzes it alongside new feedback, so a series can start years before the platform did.


Re-baselining has a visible cost, and Thematic documents it. In one[help-center example](https://help.getthematic.com/article/99-theme-discovery-changing-themes) , adding sub-themes under price raised that theme's volume from 7% to 10%. Earlier reporting on 7% now looks wrong. The history is consistent. The old slide isn't.


When the series is restated, send stakeholders a short note: what changed, the old and new figures for the affected themes, and the date.


## Step 4: Make the warehouse and BI layer survive a theme change


Plenty of teams get the platform right and break the trend downstream. Theme labels land in a warehouse table and get joined to revenue or churn data in Power BI or Tableau. Then a theme is renamed.


Three things usually go wrong:


- **Joins on theme names.** A dashboard filtered to "Delivery problems" returns nothing after the merge, or returns only the old rows.
- **Append-only loads.** New rows arrive with new labels while old rows keep old labels, so one table holds two taxonomies.
- **Changed-records-only extracts.** An incremental load picks up new comments but misses history that was re-themed in place.


Data warehousing already has words for this. The Kimball Group's[slowly changing dimensions](https://www.kimballgroup.com/2008/09/slowly-changing-dimensions-part-2/) separate Type 1, which "overwrites the changed information in the dimension," from Type 2, which adds a new dated record to preserve history. For feedback themes, the reporting table usually wants Type 1: current definitions applied to all history. If you need an audit trail too, keep a separate Type 2 table of taxonomy versions.


Thematic's[automated exports](https://getthematic.com/insights/export-themes-excel-powerpoint-bi) to Snowflake, BigQuery, and SFTP support this design. The Snowflake and BigQuery writers replicate the state of Thematic's internal table rather than patching individual records. You can also choose to export everything on each run, not only recently modified records. After a re-theme, a full export carries the restated history into the warehouse.


## Step 5: Treat an AI model change as a methodology change


The third break is one you don't make yourself. Vendors upgrade the language models behind theming, summaries, and sentiment. Thematic's article on[the upgrade trap](https://getthematic.com/insights/llm-upgrade-trap) makes the point directly: a model migration that subtly changes how themes are categorized can undermine months of trend data.


Handle it the way a survey team handles a new survey mode:


1. **Ask for notice.** The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)[AI Risk Management Framework](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/govern/) , in GOVERN 6.1, asks organizations to set policies for transparency into third-party AI systems, including training data, algorithms, and limitations. Put advance notice of model changes in the vendor contract.
2. **Run old and new in parallel.** Score one or two recent periods both ways before the switch.
3. **Restate or annotate.** If the gap is material, re-baseline history on the new model. If it isn't, annotate the switch date on the chart.


NIST GOVERN 6.2 adds a contingency process for third-party failures. For a tracker, that means naming who decides whether a shift is real.


## A worked example: one taxonomy across channels


Picture a software company with feedback arriving from support tickets, community posts, and in-app messages. If each channel gets its own coding scheme, "login problems" in support and "can't sign in" in the community become two themes with two trend lines, and every refinement has to be made and reconciled three times.


Now route all three channels into one shared taxonomy, with duplicates removed. The same theme means the same thing in every channel, and the structured results can feed a single central dashboard.


The lesson is structural. When every channel feeds one taxonomy, refining a theme means changing one frame, not reconciling several.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **A new topic model for every questionnaire revision.** Keep one frame and treat new wording as a new input.
- **Live edits to a production taxonomy.** Stage changes in a draft and release them on a schedule.
- **Splicing old and new definitions at the change date.** Re-theme the full history so the series uses one definition.
- **Re-baselining without telling anyone.** Publish old and new figures for affected themes.
- **Hard-coding theme names in BI filters and joins.** Reference themes from a mapping table, and run a full refresh after each release. Thematic's API can return themes as stable unique codes, which makes that mapping easier to maintain.
- **Assuming the vendor's AI model is fixed.** Ask how model changes are announced and tested.


## How do you keep feedback trends comparable? The short answer


Customer feedback trend lines stay comparable when the coding holds constant across questions and time, and history moves with every definition change. Thematic covers the core of this in the platform: one theme set across datasets through Lenses, draft-then-apply editing with version rollback, and automatic re-analysis of all existing feedback whenever a theme changes. The governance around it (the owner, the change note, the stakeholder notice) is still yours to run.
